steps.subtitle: and the money is cash again, ready to buy more

body.result: Around 94 days from paying for a tile to being paid for it

body.text: That last figure is the one to act on. Lantana Tiles pays its own suppliers in about 51 days, so it funds the gap between that and the 94 days out of its own pocket, every cycle, for as long as it trades.

realExample.text: A wholesaler that holds tiles for two months and waits another month to be paid has three months of trading money locked in the cycle at all times.

sections.misconception: Students describe working capital as spare money the business could spend. It is committed: most of it is tiles nobody has bought yet and invoices nobody has paid yet. A firm with $150,000 of working capital and $10,000 in the bank cannot spend $150,000.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as requiring a brief chain of reasoning. A chain about working capital runs through the cycle — a stage lengthens, money is tied up in it, less cash is available — rather than stopping at the subtraction.

recall.prompt: Lantana Tiles holds $240,000 of inventory against a cost of sales of $1,300,000, and is owed $150,000 against revenue of $2,000,000. Work the cycle out:
template: Its inventory lasts about ___
Its builders take about ___ to pay
So money is tied up in the cycle for roughly ___ before it comes back
hints: divide the inventory by the cost of sales and multiply by a year
the same idea, but against the top line rather than the cost line
the two stages of the cycle added together

sections.title: The Importance of Cash
sections.keyIdea: A business closes when it cannot pay what is due, not when it stops being profitable. Cash is the only thing that settles a bill.

body.text: The specification ends 2c with four words — **the importance of cash** — and they are the reason the whole of sub-topic 2 exists. A supplier, a landlord and a lender can all be paid in exactly one thing, and it is not profit.

Lantana Tiles has $10,000 in the bank, an overdraft of $50,000 the bank may call in, and $250,000 falling due within the year. Its profit for the year was $160,000. If the invoices arrive before the builders pay, none of that profit is available to meet them.

This is why the two documents are read together and never separately. The statement of comprehensive income says whether the trade is worth doing; the statement of financial position says whether the business can still be trading next month. A business needs both answers to be yes, and only one of them is optional in the short run.

The practical consequence is that a growing business needs more cash, not less. Every extra sale puts money into tiles and into what builders owe before it comes back, so growth consumes the cushion it is supposed to build.

realExample.text: A firm with a full order book can still be closed by a single supplier who wants paying this week and will not wait for the builders to settle next month.

sections.misconception: Students judge a business by its final profit line and treat cash as an accounting detail. The order is the other way round: a business that cannot pay stops, whatever its profit was, and the profit of a business that has stopped is of no use to anybody.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Assess as requiring a balanced chain of reasoning about competing factors that leads to a supported judgement. A judgement about whether a firm is in trouble needs both documents, and the supporting evidence for it is a figure from each.

recall.prompt: Lantana Tiles's suppliers want paying now and its builders are not due to pay for three more weeks. Complete what the firm can actually reach:
template: Of its three current assets, only ___ settles an invoice on the day
The largest of the three, at three fifths of their total, is the ___
And the profit for the year sits on the other ___ entirely
hints: the one that is already money rather than a promise of it
the one that still has to find a buyer before it becomes money
the word for the kind of thing a statement of comprehensive income is

takeaway: Profit is earned over a period; cash is what is in the bank on the day.
The statement of financial position is one date: what is owned and what is owed.
"Current" means within twelve months, on both sides.
Working capital is current assets less current liabilities, and it is committed money.

content.title: Liquidity

sections.title: The Current Ratio
sections.keyIdea: The current ratio compares what will arrive within the year with what falls due within it. Below one, the arithmetic does not work.

body.text: 2.3.3 · 2b asks for **measuring liquidity**, and the first of the two measures is the **current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities**. It expresses working capital as a ratio instead of an amount, so businesses of different sizes can be compared.
Lantana Tiles has $400,000 of current assets against $250,000 of current liabilities, so its current ratio is 1.60:1. For every dollar falling due within the year, $1.60 is expected to arrive.

Above one means the year's obligations are covered on paper. Below one means they are not, and the business is relying on something that is not on the statement — new borrowing, an owner's injection, or a sale it has not made yet.

What counts as comfortable depends entirely on how fast the current assets actually move. A wholesaler holding tiles for 67 days needs a higher ratio than a shop that sells for cash the same afternoon, because most of its current assets are a long way from being money.

realExample.text: A ratio of 1.60:1 at a firm holding two months of tiles is a different proposition from 1.60:1 at a firm holding two days of them.

sections.misconception: Students learn that a current ratio should be about two to one and apply it to every business they meet. The specification asks for the calculation and the interpretation, and the interpretation is about this firm: what its current assets are made of, and how quickly they turn into money.
sections.examMatters: Unit 2's description says the Appendix 9 ratios will not be supplied in the examination, so the formula has to be reproduced. Appendix 6 defines Calculate as a calculation from given data with workings shown, and the substitution is the working.

recall.prompt: A rival wholesaler holds $300,000 of inventory, is owed $90,000, has $30,000 in the bank and owes $300,000 within the year. Work out where it stands, in thousands of dollars:
template: Its current assets total $___ thousand
Its current ratio is therefore ___
Against Lantana Tiles's 1.60:1, that is ___ cover for the year ahead
hints: add the three things that become money within the year
divide that total by what falls due within the year
compare the two ratios and describe the rival's position

sections.title: The Acid Test Ratio
sections.keyIdea: The acid test takes inventory out of the current assets, because inventory has to be sold before it can pay anybody.

body.text: The second measure at 2b is the **acid test ratio = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities**. Appendix 9 also calls it the liquid capital ratio, and the single change from the current ratio is the one that matters: the inventory comes out.
It comes out because it is the only current asset that still has to be sold to somebody before it is money. Trade receivables are already sales; cash is already money; inventory is a hope.
Lantana Tiles has $400,000 of current assets, of which $240,000 is tiles. Take them out and $160,000 is left against $250,000 of current liabilities: an acid test of 0.64:1.

Set the two ratios side by side and they say opposite things. 1.60:1 looks safe; 0.64:1 says that without selling the tiles the firm can cover only 64% of what falls due this year. The gap between them is a measure of how much of the comfort depends on selling inventory, and for a wholesaler it is most of it.

realExample.text: A wholesaler asked to settle $250,000 tomorrow can reach $160,000 of it. The remaining $240,000 is on the racks and needs a buyer first.

sections.misconception: Students treat the acid test as a stricter version of the same measurement and quote whichever is higher. The gap between the two is the finding. A firm whose ratios are far apart is one whose liquidity depends on selling what it is holding, and that is the thing worth saying about it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as requiring a brief chain of reasoning applied to given data. Two ratios and the gap between them is data; the chain is what the gap is made of, which here is 67 days of tiles.

recall.prompt: Using Lantana Tiles's figures — $400,000 of current assets including $240,000 of inventory, and $250,000 of current liabilities — work both measures out:
template: The current ratio is ___
The acid test ratio is ___
The difference between them is entirely the ___ on the racks
hints: divide one total by the other, with nothing removed
do it again with the tiles taken out of the top
the one current asset the second measure refuses to count

sections.title: Selling Assets and Extending Supplier Credit
sections.keyIdea: The first two ways of improving liquidity do very different things: one adds money to the business, the other only delays money leaving it.

body.text: 2.3.3 · 2b names four **ways to improve liquidity, including assets, supplier credit terms, factoring, inventory JIT**. The first two are here and the other two are next. Each has to be judged on what it does to the bank balance, to working capital and to both ratios, because the four answers are not the same.

**Selling an underused asset.** Lantana Tiles sells a delivery yard it barely uses for $120,000. Cash rises to $130,000, working capital to $270,000, the current ratio to 2.08:1 and the acid test to 1.12:1: everything improves, because something that was not a current asset became one.

The cost is capacity. An asset sold is gone, and if it turns out to have been needed it must be rented back or replaced at a worse price. That is a real argument against it, and not an argument that it never works.

**Extending supplier credit terms.** Taking 30 more days to pay holds $106,849 in the bank — and adds the same $106,849 to trade payables. Working capital is unchanged at $150,000. The current ratio falls to 1.42:1 and the acid test rises to 0.75:1: adding the same amount to both sides drags every ratio towards one to one.

realExample.text: A supplier who agrees to 30 more days has lent the wholesaler $106,849 without calling it a loan — and can withdraw the offer at any time.

sections.misconception: Students write that taking longer to pay suppliers improves working capital. It does not move it: cash and the payable rise by the same amount, so the subtraction gives the same answer. What improves is the bank balance.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Discuss as requiring logical chains of reasoning in context showing causes and effects, with a brief assessment. Each of these four ways has a cost as well as an effect, and the assessment is which cost this particular firm can bear.

recall.prompt: Lantana Tiles takes 30 more days to pay its suppliers. Work out what actually moves:
template: Current assets and current liabilities both rise, by ___ amount
Working capital therefore changes by ___
And the current ratio moves from 1.60:1 to ___
hints: the money held back is money still owed, so one figure does both jobs
subtract two totals that both grew by an equal amount
divide the new current assets by the new current liabilities

sections.title: Factoring and Inventory JIT
sections.keyIdea: Factoring sells what customers owe for cash today. Inventory JIT stops money sitting on the racks. Both raise cash; only one raises the acid test.

body.text: **Factoring.** A factor buys the trade receivables and pays now, keeping a fee. Lantana Tiles sells its $150,000 of receivables for a 3% fee of $4,500, so $145,500 arrives and the bank balance goes from $10,000 to $155,500.

Look at what it does to the ratios, though. One quick asset has become another, minus the fee, so working capital falls by exactly the $4,500 and the acid test edges down from 0.64:1 to 0.62:1. Factoring is the move that rescues the bank balance while very slightly worsening the measure of liquidity — which is the clearest proof in the topic that a ratio is not the same thing as being able to pay.

**Inventory JIT.** Ordering tiles so they arrive as they are needed cuts inventory from 67 days of cover to 30 days, releasing $133,151 of cash. Current assets do not change — tiles became cash — so working capital and the current ratio stay exactly where they were, while the acid test jumps from 0.64:1 to 1.17:1.
Its cost is fragility. A business holding 30 days of tiles has no buffer against a supplier who is late, which is one of the external causes of failure the next chapter reaches.

realExample.text: Two wholesalers both raise about $133,151 of cash. The one that factored still holds its tiles; the one on JIT has nothing on the racks if a ship is delayed.

sections.misconception: Students rank the four ways from best to worst. They do different jobs: one adds an asset, one delays a payment, one converts a receivable, one releases inventory. The right question is which measure this firm needs to move, and what it can afford to give up to move it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Evaluate as requiring fully developed chains of reasoning and a full awareness of competing factors, leading to a perceptive conclusion proposing a recommendation. Four options with four different costs is what that command word is built for.

recall.prompt: Match each way of improving liquidity to what it does to the acid test ratio:

pairs.why: A non-current asset turns into cash, so the top of the ratio grows while the bottom does not move at all.
One quick asset is exchanged for another and the factor keeps a fee, so the top falls by exactly that fee.

pairs.left: Cutting inventory to 30 days of cover
pairs.why: Tiles are not counted in this ratio and cash is, so releasing inventory moves money from the part that is ignored to the part that counts.

pairs.left: Taking 30 more days to pay suppliers
pairs.why: Cash and payables rise together, and adding the same amount to both sides pulls a ratio below one upwards towards one to one.

takeaway: Current ratio is current assets over current liabilities. Acid test drops the inventory.
The gap between the two measures how much comfort depends on selling inventory.
The four ways the specification names do four different things.
Longer supplier credit leaves working capital unchanged and drags ratios towards one to one.

content.title: Business Failure

sections.title: Poor Cash Flow Management and Overtrading
sections.keyIdea: Most failures are not caused by losses. They are caused by running out of money while still trading profitably.

body.text: 2.3.3 · 3a lists six **internal causes of business failure**, and the specification puts **poor management of cash flow** first. It is first because it is the mechanism most of the others end in: whatever goes wrong, the business closes on the day it cannot pay.

Poor management of cash flow is not the same as making a loss. It is letting money go out faster than it comes in — paying suppliers before customers pay, buying assets outright that could have been paid for over time, holding tiles for 67 days when builders pay in 27 days.

**Overtrading** is the version of this that happens to successful businesses, and the specification names it separately. A firm grows faster than its working capital can support: every extra sale buys inventory and creates a receivable before any money comes back.

If Lantana Tiles grew by 50%, inventory would rise by $120,000 and trade receivables by $75,000, while trade payables would only rise by $90,000. That is $105,000 of extra money needed, from a business with $10,000 in the bank whose trading produced no spare cash at all this year.

realExample.text: A wholesaler that wins a large contract and cannot fund the tiles for it has been destroyed by good news, which is precisely what makes overtrading hard to see coming.

sections.misconception: Students treat growth as the answer to a cash problem. Growth consumes cash before it produces any: it is the fastest way to turn a tight position into an impossible one, and a firm should fund the growth before it accepts the order.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Assess as a balanced and wide-ranging chain of reasoning about competing factors leading to a supported judgement. A case with rising revenue and falling cash is asking which of the two is the more reliable signal, and the judgement has to say why.

recall.prompt: A rival holding $200,000 of inventory, owed $100,000 and owing suppliers $120,000 is offered enough work to double its trade. Everything scales with it. Work out what the growth costs, in thousands of dollars:
template: More money tied up in inventory and trade receivables: $___ thousand
Less needed straight away, because trade payables also rise: $___ thousand
So the funding the growth needs before any of it is paid for is $___ thousand
hints: double each of the two current assets that grow with the trade, and take the increase
the same again on what the firm owes its suppliers
the first figure less the second

sections.title: Overestimation of Sales and Poor Inventory Control
sections.keyIdea: Buying for sales that never happen turns cash into tiles. Both of these causes are the same mistake at different points in the cycle.

body.text: **Overestimation of sales** is the second internal cause at 3a. A business forecasts more than it will sell and commits to it: it buys the goods, takes the space, hires the people. The cash goes out on the strength of the forecast and the revenue does not arrive.

If Lantana Tiles bought in for 25% more trade than it achieved, $325,000 of extra tiles would be sitting on the racks — more than twice its entire working capital of $150,000. Tiles go out of fashion, so if a quarter of that never sells, $81,250 is written off, which is 40.6% of the year's operating profit.

**Poor inventory control** is the fourth cause, and the same damage without a bad forecast. Holding too much means cash in tiles rather than the bank, storage to pay for and breakages to absorb. Holding too little means turning builders away to a rival who had the tiles.

Lantana Tiles holds 67 days of cover; getting that to 30 days would release $133,151. That is inventory JIT from the liquidity chapter seen from the other end: good inventory control and improving liquidity are one action with two names.

realExample.text: A pattern that stops selling is worth what somebody will pay for it, which is usually a fraction of what it cost. Until it is sold, it is counted as an asset at full value.

sections.misconception: Students treat unsold inventory as harmless because it is still an asset on the statement. It is an asset that is not earning anything, that cost cash the business no longer has, and that may be worth far less than its stated value the moment anyone tries to sell it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Explain as requiring a brief explanation of cause or effect supported by details or examples. One cause, its route through the working capital cycle, and its effect on the bank balance is the chain the marks are for.

recall.prompt: A rival with a cost of sales of $800,000 buys in for half as much trade again as it achieves, and a fifth of the excess never sells. Work out the damage, in thousands of dollars:
template: Goods left over at the end of the year: $___ thousand
Written off when a fifth of them never sell: $___ thousand
The rest is not a loss, but it is cash the firm cannot ___
hints: half again on what the goods actually sold cost
a fifth of the figure above
the verb for what you cannot do with money that is sitting in goods

sections.title: Poor Marketing and Poor Quality
sections.keyIdea: Poor marketing costs a business customers it never hears about. Poor quality costs it the ones it already has, and costs it twice.

body.text: The last two internal causes at 3a are **poor marketing** and **poor quality**. Both act on the top of the statement, and they act differently enough to be worth separating.

**Poor marketing** means customers who would have bought do not know the business exists, or no longer think of it. Revenue falls while the costs of running the business do not. If Lantana Tiles lost 15% of its volume this way, operating profit would fall from $200,000 to $95,000, because the $500,000 of operating expenses carries on regardless.

**Poor quality** costs twice over. The immediate cost is replacing what was wrong: if 3% of tiles arrive broken and are replaced free, cost of sales rises by $39,000 and operating profit falls to $161,000 — a fall of 19.5% from a 3% breakage rate.

The second cost is the one that closes businesses. A builder who has had a bad delivery does not order again and tells other builders, so the quality problem becomes a marketing problem a year later — and by then no amount of advertising fixes it, because what customers heard was true.

realExample.text: A wholesaler with a 3% breakage rate loses $39,000 in replacements, and loses the builders who now specify a different supplier in every quotation.

sections.misconception: Students treat marketing and quality as soft causes next to the financial ones. Both land on the statement as hard numbers, and quality is the more dangerous because its full cost arrives long after the problem was fixed.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Analyse as requiring a brief chain of reasoning applied to given data. A chain that runs from a breakage rate through cost of sales to operating profit uses the data; naming the cause and asserting the business suffers does not.

recall.prompt: Six causes of failure are listed. Decide which line of the statement of comprehensive income each one hits first, by sorting them into these groups:

groups.name: Hits revenue first
items: Customers stop hearing from the firm
Goods were bought in for orders that never came
groups.why: Both are failures to sell what the firm expected to sell, so the top line falls while every cost below it carries on.

groups.name: Hits cost of sales first
items: Deliveries reach the builder cracked and are sent again
Patterns nobody wanted are written down at the year end
groups.why: Replacing what was wrong and writing down what will not sell both raise what the goods sold have cost, which is the second line down.

groups.name: Hits neither, but empties the bank
items: Trade doubles faster than the money to fund it
Suppliers are settled long before customers pay
groups.why: Neither changes a single line of the statement of comprehensive income: the trade is profitable and the money is tied up in the cycle instead of in the bank.

sections.title: Market Conditions, Competition and the Economy
sections.keyIdea: External causes are not the firm's fault and are still its problem. The first three all arrive as a fall in what it can sell or charge.

body.text: 3b lists eight **external causes of business failure**, beginning with **market conditions**, **competition** and **economic** conditions. None of them is inside the firm's control, and each of them reaches the statement through the top line.

**Market conditions.** Demand for the product itself changes: builders stop building, or tastes move. A 10% fall in volume takes Lantana Tiles's operating profit from $200,000 to $130,000, because the $500,000 of operating expenses does not fall with the trade.

**Competition.** A rival takes customers, or forces the price down. This one is the sharpest: a 5% price cut with exactly the same tiles sold leaves cost of sales untouched and takes operating profit to $100,000 — half of it. Price cuts fall straight through to the profit line, which is why a price war closes businesses faster than a downturn.

**Economic** conditions are the general background: incomes, employment and confidence across the whole economy rather than in one trade. They matter here because they move several things at once, and because a business cannot wait them out without cash.

realExample.text: A wholesaler can survive builders ordering a tenth less. Matching a rival's price cut of a twentieth on every tile costs it the same amount again, and it has not lost a single customer.

sections.misconception: Students treat external causes as an excuse, and write that a firm failed "because of the recession" as though nothing else were relevant. Every firm in the trade faced the same conditions and some of them are still open. The question is always what made this one unable to absorb it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Assess as requiring a balanced and wide-ranging chain of reasoning about competing factors, leading to a supported judgement. Assessing a failure means weighing an external cause against the internal position it landed on.

recall.prompt: A rival with revenue of $1,000,000, cost of sales of $600,000 and operating expenses of $300,000 meets two shocks. Work both out, in thousands of dollars:
template: A 10% fall in the volume it sells leaves an operating profit of $___ thousand
A 5% cut in its price, with volumes unchanged, leaves $___ thousand
The smaller-sounding shock is therefore the ___ one
hints: revenue and cost of sales both fall by a tenth; the operating expenses do not
revenue alone falls, by a twentieth, with both costs unchanged
compare the two figures and describe the price cut

sections.title: Exchange Rates and Interest Rates
sections.keyIdea: A currency movement hits an importer at the cost of sales. An interest rate rise is the one cause that leaves operating profit untouched.

body.text: The next two external causes at 3b are **exchange rates** and **interest rates**. They are grouped here because they arrive from the same direction and land on completely different lines.

**Exchange rates.** Lantana Tiles buys its tiles abroad. If the home currency falls 10% against the currency the tiles are priced in, they cost 10% more: cost of sales rises to $1,430,000 and operating profit falls from $200,000 to $70,000, which is 65% of it gone.
The same movement helps an exporter, which is why the effect has to be worked out for the firm in front of you rather than recalled.

**Interest rates.** Lantana Tiles owes $500,000 at 8%. A rise of 4 percentage points takes the interest to $60,000 and the profit for the year from $160,000 to $140,000 — while the operating profit does not move at all, because interest comes off below it.
That is the whole reason the ladder has three rungs. A business hit by rates trades exactly as well as it did the week before, and only one of its three profit figures says so.

realExample.text: An importer and an exporter in the same street read the same currency news and one of them is in trouble. Which one depends on which side of the statement the foreign currency sits on.

sections.misconception: Students learn "a weaker currency helps exporters" and apply it to every firm. For an importer it is the opposite, and for a business that imports its goods and sells them at home the entire effect lands on cost of sales with nothing offsetting it.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Calculate as a calculation based on given data with workings given. A currency question is a percentage on one line of the statement, so the working is the line it lands on as much as the arithmetic.

recall.prompt: Four shocks hit the importer. Decide for each which profit figures move, by sorting them into these groups:

groups.name: Moves operating profit
items: The local currency weakens against the one the goods are priced in
A competitor forces a price cut
The landlord raises the rent on the premises
groups.why: Each of these changes revenue or a cost above the operating profit line, so that figure and the one below it both move.

groups.name: Leaves operating profit unchanged
items: The rate on the bank loan rises
The firm takes out a second loan
groups.why: Interest is the only thing taken off between operating profit and profit for the year, so anything about borrowing leaves the trading figures exactly where they were.

sections.title: Regulation, Supplier Problems and Natural Phenomena
sections.keyIdea: The last three external causes arrive without warning, and a business survives them out of its cash rather than out of its profit.

body.text: 3b ends with **government regulations**, **supplier problems** and **natural phenomena**. None can be forecast from the trade itself, and what decides the outcome is the same in all three: how long the business can keep paying while it is disrupted.

**Government regulations.** A new rule can close a product line overnight. If a building standard changed and a quarter of Lantana Tiles's inventory no longer met it, $60,000 would be scrapped — against a bank balance of $10,000.

**Supplier problems.** A factory that stops delivering stops the wholesaler too. Lantana Tiles sells about $8,000 on each of 250 trading days, so 20 days without tiles costs $160,000 of revenue and takes operating profit to $144,000, every expense carrying on.

**Natural phenomena.** A flood, a storm or an earthquake closes premises and destroys what is in them. The $240,000 on the racks is at risk in a single night, and insurance pays later rather than now.

So the last three make the same argument as the first: what a business needs against an external shock is liquidity. Profit is what it earns when things go normally, and none of these three is normal.

realExample.text: Two identical wholesalers are flooded on the same night. The one that had cut its inventory and held cash reopens; the one with $240,000 of tiles on the floor and $10,000 in the bank does not.

sections.misconception: Students write that a firm hit by a disaster or a new rule "could not have done anything about it". It could not have prevented the event; it could have been able to survive it. That is what the liquidity chapter was for.
sections.examMatters: Appendix 6 defines Evaluate as requiring fully developed chains of reasoning and a full awareness of competing factors leading to a perceptive conclusion that proposes a recommendation. A failure case usually has an external trigger and an internal reason it was fatal, and a conclusion has to say which was decisive.

recall.prompt: Put the stages of a business failure in causal order, from the first event to the closure:
correctOrder: A supplier stops delivering for three weeks
Revenue stops while rent and salaries carry on
The bank balance runs down and the overdraft limit is reached
An invoice falls due that the business cannot pay
why: The external shock comes first and the business has done nothing wrong at this point.
Its costs are not suspended because its sales are, so the gap between money in and money out opens immediately.
The cushion absorbs the gap for as long as it lasts, and how long that is was decided months earlier by how much cash the firm held.
Failure is this moment and not the shock that started it, which is why a liquid business survives the same event.

takeaway: Six internal causes and eight external ones, and all of them end in the same place.
A business closes when it cannot pay, not when it stops being profitable.
Interest rates are the only cause that leaves operating profit untouched.
Growth consumes cash before it produces any, which is overtrading.

notes.title: Profit
notes.keyIdea: Three profits on one ladder, the costs that come off at each step, and the document that sets them out.

items.text: Gross profit — revenue less cost of sales. Only the goods sold come off.
Operating profit — gross profit less other operating expenses. Before interest.
Profit for the year (net profit) — operating profit less interest. What the owners keep.
Statement of comprehensive income — the ladder as a document, covering a period of trading.
Lantana Tiles: revenue $2,000,000 → gross $700,000 → operating $200,000 → profit for the year $160,000.
There is no tax line in the specification's own statement (Appendix 9), so nothing is worked out after tax.
A data table with no interest figure can support an operating profit and cannot support a profit for the year.

takeaway: Ask which profit before calculating anything.
Cost of sales is the goods, not the office.
Net profit and profit for the year are one line.

notes.title: Profitability
notes.keyIdea: Three margins, the gap each one measures, and why an action can raise profit while lowering profitability.

items.text: Gross profit margin — (gross profit ÷ revenue) × 100. Buying and pricing.
Operating profit margin — (operating profit ÷ revenue) × 100. The whole trading operation, before financing.
Profit for the year margin — (profit for the year ÷ revenue) × 100. After the lenders.
Lantana Tiles: 35%, then 10%, then 8%. The first gap is the overheads; the second is the $40,000 of interest.
A 5% price cut with volumes unchanged takes operating profit from $200,000 to $100,000: price changes fall straight through.
Cutting a price and selling much more can raise the profit and lower every margin. Profit is an amount; profitability is a rate.

takeaway: Every margin has revenue underneath it.
Say which gap moved, not which margin is lowest.
Growth usually raises profit and lowers profitability.

notes.title: Cash and the Statement of Financial Position
notes.keyIdea: Why a profitable year can end with less money, what the second document holds, and what working capital actually is.

items.text: Statement of financial position — what is owned and owed on one date.
Current assets — inventory, trade receivables and cash: money within twelve months.
Current liabilities — trade payables, overdraft and other payables: owed within twelve months.
Working capital — current assets less current liabilities.
$160,000 of profit and a cash movement of −$100,000: inventory up $90,000, receivables up $60,000, payables up $70,000, a $100,000 asset bought and $80,000 of loan repaid.
The cycle: cash buys inventory (67 days), inventory becomes trade receivables (27 days), receivables become cash.
Working capital of $150,000 against $10,000 in the bank: the cushion is real and almost none of it is spendable.

takeaway: A sale on credit is profit today and cash next month.
Repaying a loan costs cash and is not an expense.
Growth consumes working capital before it produces any.

notes.title: Liquidity
notes.keyIdea: Two ratios, the gap between them, and what each of the four ways of improving liquidity actually moves.

items.text: Current ratio — current assets ÷ current liabilities.
Acid test ratio — (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities. Appendix 9 also calls it the liquid capital ratio.
Factoring — selling trade receivables to a factor for cash now, less a fee.
Lantana Tiles: 1.60:1 and 0.64:1. The whole gap is $240,000 of tiles, about 67 days of cover.

Sell an asset: everything improves. Extend supplier credit: working capital unchanged, ratios dragged towards 1:1. Factoring: cash to $155,500, acid test down to 0.62:1. Inventory JIT: acid test to 1.17:1, current ratio unchanged.
Adding the same amount to current assets and current liabilities leaves working capital alone and moves every ratio towards one to one.

takeaway: Interpret a ratio against what the current assets are made of.
Longer supplier credit does not improve working capital.
Factoring raises the cash and lowers the acid test.

notes.title: Business Failure
notes.keyIdea: Six internal causes and eight external ones, each priced on the line of the statement it lands on.

items.text: Internal causes — poor management of cash flow, overestimation of sales, overtrading, poor inventory control, poor marketing, poor quality.
External causes — market conditions, competition, economic, exchange rates, interest rates, government regulations, supplier problems, natural phenomena.
Overtrading — growing faster than the working capital can fund.
Competition, a 5% price cut: operating profit $100,000. Exchange rates, a 10% fall for an importer: $70,000. Market conditions, 10% less volume: $130,000.
Interest rates, 4 points on $500,000: operating profit unchanged, profit for the year $140,000.
Growing 50% needs $105,000 of extra funding before any of it is paid for.
Every cause ends at the same place: an invoice falls due and the money is not there.

takeaway: Name the line of the statement the cause lands on.
A price cut costs more than a bigger fall in volume.
The shock is the trigger; the liquidity decides the outcome.

quiz.question: Gross profit is calculated as:
options: revenue less all of the costs of running the business
revenue less cost of sales and interest
revenue less cost of sales
the profit left for the owners at the end of the year
quiz.explanation: Only what the goods sold cost to obtain comes off at this step. Taking the running costs off as well produces the operating profit, and taking interest off as well produces the profit for the year, so each of the other three describes a rung further down the ladder.

quiz.question: Which figure does the specification also call net profit?
options: Profit for the year
Operating profit
Gross profit
Revenue less cost of sales
quiz.explanation: The leaf is written as "profit for the year (net profit)", so the two names label one line: the figure left after interest. Operating profit sits one rung above it and is the same number only for a business that has borrowed nothing.

quiz.question: A statement of comprehensive income differs from a statement of financial position because it:
options: covers a period of trading rather than a single date
lists what a business owns rather than what it earns
is prepared only by businesses that have borrowed
shows cash movements rather than profit
quiz.explanation: One is a record of flows between two dates and the other is a photograph taken on one. That is why a question containing the word "during" is about the statement of comprehensive income and a question about what is held or owed is about the statement of financial position.

quiz.question: A wholesaler reports revenue of $2,000,000, cost of sales of $1,300,000 and other operating expenses of $500,000. No interest figure is given. The largest profit that can be worked out from this is:
options: a profit for the year of $200,000
a gross profit of $700,000
a profit for the year of $160,000
an operating profit of $200,000
quiz.explanation: The ladder stops where the data stops. Both subtractions the table supports can be made, and taking the other operating expenses off as well gives the operating profit; the rung below needs an interest figure, and inventing one to reach it is answering a question the data was never able to ask.

quiz.question: Which of these belongs in cost of sales for a tile wholesaler?
options: The salary of the warehouse manager
The rent paid on the warehouse
The shipping paid to bring the tiles into the warehouse
The interest paid on the warehouse loan
quiz.explanation: Cost of sales is what the goods that were sold cost to obtain, freight included. The other three are owed whichever tiles were sold and in most years whether any were, so they sit below the gross profit line — and the interest below the operating profit line as well.

quiz.question: Two wholesalers trade identically, but one has borrowed heavily and the other has not. They will report:
options: the same profit for the year and different operating profits
the same operating profit and different profits for the year
different figures on every line of the statement
identical statements, because interest is not a cost
quiz.explanation: Interest comes off between the two figures, so everything above it is untouched by how the business was financed. That is exactly why the operating line is the fair one for comparing firms and the line beneath it is not.

quiz.question: Lantana Tiles pays $40,000 of interest on a loan of $500,000. The rate it is paying is:
quiz.explanation: The rate is the interest divided by the amount borrowed — $40,000 over $500,000, which is 8%. Dividing the interest by revenue instead gives 2%, and 35% is the gross profit margin: a rate on borrowing has the amount borrowed underneath it, not the sales.

quiz.question: The specification's own statement of comprehensive income contains no line for:
options: interest
tax
cost of sales
other operating expenses
quiz.explanation: Appendix 9 runs revenue, cost of sales, gross profit, other operating expenses, operating profit, interest, profit for the year, and stops. A figure worked out after tax is a figure no data table on this paper will ask for or supply.

quiz.question: Lantana Tiles has a gross profit of $700,000 on revenue of $2,000,000. Its gross profit margin is:
quiz.explanation: The margin divides the profit by the revenue and multiplies by a hundred. Dividing by cost of sales instead gives 53.8%, a number that compares with nothing because nobody else calculates it that way, and 65% is the cost of sales as a share of revenue rather than the profit.

quiz.question: The gap between a firm's gross profit margin and its operating profit margin is a measure of:
options: what the goods themselves cost, as a share of revenue
the cost of the firm's borrowing
how quickly the firm collects what it is owed
what running the business costs, as a share of revenue
quiz.explanation: Only the other operating expenses come off between those two lines, so the distance between the margins is exactly those expenses expressed as a rate. The cost of the goods is the gap above, and the cost of borrowing is the gap below.

quiz.question: A wholesaler cuts its price by 5% and sells exactly as many tiles. Its operating profit:
options: is unchanged, because the same tiles were sold
falls to $100,000, because no cost fell with the price
falls by 5%, in line with the price
falls to $130,000, in line with the revenue lost
quiz.explanation: Revenue falls by $100,000 and both costs stay where they were, so the whole reduction lands on the profit line. A twentieth off the price has taken half the operating profit, which is why price is the most dangerous lever a business has.

quiz.question: A firm cuts its price, sells far more, and reports a higher operating profit with a lower operating profit margin. This shows that:
options: the calculation contains an error somewhere
the firm has become more efficient at buying
the extra sales were made at a loss
profit is an amount and profitability is a rate
quiz.explanation: Revenue and cost of sales both grew, so the amount kept rose while the share of each dollar kept fell. Nothing is wrong and nothing was sold at a loss: the business is simply working harder for every dollar it now earns.

quiz.question: Which action raises the profit amount and lowers every margin?
options: Cutting the price and selling considerably more
Dropping the product line with the smallest margin
Negotiating a lower price from the supplier
Repaying part of the loan early
quiz.explanation: Only cutting the price and selling considerably more grows revenue and cost of sales together. Dropping a weak line and buying better both widen a gap on the statement rather than lengthening it, and repaying a loan cannot touch the two trading margins at all.

quiz.question: Lantana Tiles earned $160,000 of profit for the year and its bank balance fell by $100,000. The most likely explanation is that it:
options: made an arithmetic error in one of the statements
bought inventory and assets, and sold on credit
paid the whole profit out to its owners
was trading at a loss for most of the year
quiz.explanation: Profit is recorded when a sale is made and cash moves when money changes hands, so a year of buying tiles, buying equipment and waiting to be paid can easily consume more cash than the trade produced. Both figures are correct and they are measuring different things.

quiz.question: Repaying part of a bank loan has what effect on the statement of comprehensive income?
options: None, because repaying borrowed money is not a cost
It reduces the profit for the year by the amount repaid
It reduces the operating profit by the amount repaid
It reduces the gross profit by the amount repaid
quiz.explanation: Only the interest on borrowing is a cost; returning the sum borrowed simply reduces what is owed. The money certainly leaves the bank, which is the whole point of the distinction between profit and cash.

quiz.question: Which of these is a current liability?
options: A bank loan repayable in four years
The warehouse the business trades from
A supplier invoice due in six weeks
Tiles waiting on the racks to be sold
quiz.explanation: "Current" means falling due within twelve months, so the six-week invoice qualifies and the four-year loan does not. The other two are assets rather than liabilities, and one of them is not even a current asset.

quiz.question: Lantana Tiles has current assets of $400,000 and current liabilities of $250,000. Its working capital is:
quiz.explanation: Working capital is one subtraction: what arrives within the year less what falls due within it. It is not the current assets on their own, and it is certainly not the $10,000 actually in the bank, most of the cushion being tiles and unpaid invoices.

quiz.question: A business with working capital of $150,000 and $10,000 in the bank:
options: can pay an invoice today up to $150,000
can pay an invoice today only up to $10,000
has no liquidity problem of any kind
is trading at a loss
quiz.explanation: Working capital is a cushion and most of it is committed: tiles nobody has bought and invoices nobody has paid. Only one line on the statement of financial position settles a bill on the day, and it is the smallest of the three current assets here.

quiz.question: A wholesaler holds $240,000 of inventory, is owed $150,000, has $10,000 in the bank and owes $250,000 within the year. Its acid test ratio is:
quiz.explanation: The acid test takes the inventory out of the top and leaves $160,000 against $250,000. Leaving the tiles in gives the current ratio instead, which is the same arithmetic answering a much less demanding question.

quiz.question: Inventory is excluded from the acid test ratio because it:
options: is usually worth more than the statement says
is not owned outright until the supplier is paid
must be sold to somebody before it becomes money
cannot be counted as an asset at all
quiz.explanation: Trade receivables are sales already made and cash is already money; inventory is neither. It is the one current asset with a further transaction standing between it and the bank account, which is exactly what the stricter measure is testing for.

quiz.question: A firm takes 30 more days to pay its suppliers, holding $106,849 in the bank. Its working capital:
options: does not change, because cash and trade payables rise together
rises by $106,849, because the cash is in the bank
falls by $106,849, because more is owed
rises, because the current ratio improves
quiz.explanation: Both sides of the subtraction grow by the same amount, so the answer to it is the same as before. What does change is the current ratio, which falls from 1.60:1 to 1.42:1: adding equal amounts to both sides drags every ratio towards one to one.

quiz.question: Factoring $150,000 of trade receivables for a 3% fee takes the bank balance to $155,500. Its effect on the acid test ratio is that it:
options: rises sharply, because there is far more cash
does not move, because nothing left the business
falls slightly, from 0.64:1 to 0.62:1
rises to 1.17:1, the same as cutting inventory would
quiz.explanation: Both trade receivables and cash are already counted in the measure, so one quick asset has simply become another — minus the fee, which is the only real change. It is the clearest proof in the topic that being able to pay and scoring well on a ratio are different things.

quiz.question: Cutting inventory from 67 days of cover to 30 days releases $133,151 of cash. The current ratio afterwards is:
options: unchanged at 1.60:1
higher, at 2.08:1
higher, at 1.17:1
lower, at 1.42:1
quiz.explanation: Tiles became cash and both are current assets, so the top of the ratio is exactly what it was and the bottom has not moved either. The acid test is the measure that responds, because it counts one of those two assets and refuses the other.

quiz.question: Overtrading means that a business:
options: sells its goods below what they cost to buy
borrows more than its assets are worth
grows faster than its working capital can fund
trades in more countries than it can manage
quiz.explanation: Every extra sale buys inventory and creates a receivable before any money comes back, so growth consumes cash ahead of producing it. It is the cause of failure that happens to businesses whose order books are full, which is what makes it hard to see coming.

quiz.question: If Lantana Tiles grew 50% on the same terms, the extra funding it would need before any of the growth was paid for is:
quiz.explanation: Inventory rises $120,000 and trade receivables $75,000, while trade payables supply $90,000 of it. The difference has to come from somewhere, and a year that produced no spare cash is not that somewhere.

quiz.question: An importer's home currency falls 10% against the currency its goods are priced in. The line of its statement that moves first is:
options: revenue
cost of sales
other operating expenses
interest
quiz.explanation: The same goods now cost more to buy, so cost of sales rises from $1,300,000 to $1,430,000 and every profit beneath it falls. An exporter facing the same movement would see it arrive at the top line instead, and in the opposite direction.

quiz.question: A rise in interest rates is unusual among the causes of business failure because it:
options: affects only businesses that are already unprofitable
cannot be planned for in any way
leaves the operating profit completely unchanged
reduces revenue rather than raising a cost
quiz.explanation: Interest is taken off between operating profit and profit for the year, so a business hit by rates is trading exactly as well as it was the week before. That is the whole reason the specification's ladder separates the two figures.

quiz.question: Two identical wholesalers are hit by the same three-week supplier failure and only one of them closes. The difference between them is most likely:
options: which of them had the higher profit last year
which of them had the larger warehouse
which of them had the better relationship with the supplier
how much cash each had when the deliveries stopped
quiz.explanation: The shock was identical, so what separates them is the ability to keep paying while no revenue arrives. Last year's profit settles no invoices, and a bigger warehouse is a non-current asset that cannot be turned into money in three weeks.

practice.question: Define the term 'profit for the year'. (2 marks)
practice.guidance:
Two marks means two separate things to say, and the second is not a rewording of the first. Settle first which figure it is measured from, and then what has been taken off to reach it. An answer that says "the profit a business makes" has said neither.
Profit for the year is the profit remaining after interest has been deducted from operating profit (1 mark), and it is the figure available to the owners of the business (1 mark). The specification also calls it net profit, and either name is acceptable. An answer that describes it as the profit after all costs, without naming interest or the line it is measured from, has given one general statement rather than two specific ones.

practice.question: A tile wholesaler reports, for the year: revenue $2,000,000, cost of sales $1,300,000, other operating expenses $500,000, interest $40,000. Calculate the wholesaler's gross profit, operating profit and profit for the year. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Work down the ladder in the specification's own order rather than reaching for the figure the question names last. Each line you produce is the starting point for the next, so setting them out in sequence is both the method and the workings. Label each figure: three unlabelled numbers cannot be told apart.
Gross profit = revenue − cost of sales = $700,000 (1 mark). Operating profit = gross profit − other operating expenses = $200,000 (1 mark). Profit for the year = operating profit − interest = $160,000 (1 mark). A further mark is available for correctly labelled workings that show the three subtractions in order. An answer that reaches $160,000 with no intermediate lines has produced the right figure and shown none of the method the question asked for.

practice.question: A tile wholesaler reports, for the year: revenue $2,000,000, cost of sales $1,300,000, other operating expenses $500,000, interest $40,000. Calculate the wholesaler's gross profit margin and its operating profit margin. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
The two profits have to exist before the two margins can, so the first part of this is the calculation you have already met. Then be careful about what goes underneath: every margin in the specification has the same figure below the line, and it is not the one you just subtracted. Give each answer as a percentage.
Gross profit margin = ($700,000 ÷ $2,000,000) × 100 = 35% (2 marks: one for the correct gross profit, one for the margin). Operating profit margin = ($200,000 ÷ $2,000,000) × 100 = 10% (2 marks, on the same basis). Dividing by cost of sales rather than revenue gives 53.8% and 15.4%; those figures compare with nothing and score no marks for the margin, although a correctly calculated profit still scores.

practice.question: A tile wholesaler is pushed by a competitor into cutting its prices by 5%. It expects to sell exactly the same quantity of tiles as before. Analyse the likely effect on its profitability. (6 marks)
practice.guidance:
This wants one chain, followed through, not a list of everything a price cut touches. Start by settling which lines of the statement move and which do not, because that is what makes the effect larger than the percentage suggests. Then carry the consequence down to the measure the question names rather than stopping at the profit figure.
The chain: a price cut reduces revenue while the quantity sold is unchanged, so cost of sales is unaffected; the whole reduction therefore falls on gross profit and passes through to operating profit, which drops from $200,000 to $100,000. Because revenue has also fallen, the operating profit margin falls from 10% to 5.3%. The strongest answers note that a 5% movement in price has removed about half the operating profit, and that this is a property of price cuts generally: no cost falls alongside them. Appendix 6 defines Analyse as a brief chain of reasoning and states that it does not require evaluation, so a judgement about whether the firm should have cut its price is not what is being asked for here.

practice.question: Construct a labelled diagram of the working capital cycle for a wholesaler that buys goods, sells them on credit and collects payment. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Decide first what the four stages are and which direction the arrows run, because a cycle drawn as a list is not a cycle. Every stage needs a label in the vocabulary of the statement of financial position rather than in everyday words. Show where the money is at each point, not just what the business is doing.
A correct diagram is a closed loop with four labelled stages and arrows running one way: cash, then inventory, then trade receivables, then cash again (2 marks for the four correctly named stages, 1 mark for the loop closing and the arrows running consistently). A further mark is available for annotating the stages with a duration or an amount, showing that money is tied up for the length of the cycle. Appendix 6 defines Construct as requiring an accurately labelled diagram, so an unlabelled loop, however correct its shape, cannot receive the labelling marks.

practice.question: A wholesaler reports a healthy profit for the year and its bank balance falls over the same period. Explain one reason why this can happen. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
One reason, developed, beats four reasons named. Choose a mechanism where the timing of the money and the timing of the record genuinely differ, and then follow it from the transaction to the bank balance. Saying that profit and cash are different things is the claim rather than the explanation.
Any one of these, developed: selling on credit records the revenue when the sale is made while the cash arrives later, so a growing business is continually owed more than it has collected (up to 4 marks); buying inventory that has not yet been sold takes cash out without any cost being recorded, because the goods are still an asset; buying a non-current asset outright removes cash and is not an expense at all; repaying borrowed money reduces what is owed and is not a cost, only the interest being one. Appendix 6 defines Explain as requiring a brief explanation of cause or effect supported by details or examples, so the marks are for following one mechanism through rather than for the number of mechanisms named.

practice.question: A tile wholesaler's statement of financial position shows: inventory $240,000, trade receivables $150,000, cash $10,000, trade payables $180,000, bank overdraft $50,000, other payables $20,000, non-current assets $900,000, bank loan repayable in five years $500,000. Calculate the wholesaler's current ratio and its acid test ratio. (4 marks)
practice.guidance:
Before any arithmetic, sort the figures you have been given: some of them belong in this calculation and some are there to see whether you know they do not. The test in both cases is the same word, and it appears on both sides of each ratio. Then remember what the second measure removes and why.
Current assets = $240,000 + $150,000 + $10,000 = $400,000; current liabilities = $180,000 + $50,000 + $20,000 = $250,000 (1 mark for each total). Current ratio = $400,000 ÷ $250,000 = 1.60:1 (1 mark). Acid test = ($400,000 − $240,000) ÷ $250,000 = 0.64:1 (1 mark). The non-current assets and the five-year loan belong in neither calculation; including them gives 1.73:1 and answers a question nobody asked.

practice.question: A wholesaler with a weak bank balance is advised to negotiate an extra month of credit from its suppliers. Discuss whether this would improve its liquidity. (8 marks)
practice.guidance:
The advice is partly right and partly wrong, so decide first what "improve its liquidity" would actually mean here: a better bank balance, a larger cushion, or a better ratio. Work out what happens to each of those separately, because they do not all move the same way. Then weigh what the firm gives up by owing its suppliers for longer.
Level 1 describes supplier credit without applying it to the firm. Level 2 builds one chain: the money held back raises the bank balance, which is the immediate problem solved. Level 3 builds the competing chain and reaches the brief assessment Appendix 6 states the command word requires — the same amount is added to trade payables, so working capital is unchanged at $150,000 and the current ratio falls from 1.60:1 to 1.42:1, while the acid test rises from 0.64:1 to 0.75:1, because adding equal amounts to both sides drags every ratio towards one to one; and against the advice, the credit can be withdrawn at any time, the supplier may raise prices or stop prioritising the firm, and nothing in the cycle itself has been fixed, so the problem returns next month. The assessment has to say whether the advice is sound for this firm rather than list both sides.

practice.question: Assess the importance of managing liquidity for a small wholesaler whose sales are growing rapidly. (10 marks)
practice.guidance:
Growth is the complication here, so the answer has to explain why a business selling more can be in more danger rather than less. Work out what a growing firm needs more of before the extra money arrives, and then weigh that against the arguments on the other side — the things a business would give up by holding liquidity it does not need. The question asks how important, which means the answer has to end somewhere rather than balance forever.
Level 1 covers a description of liquidity or of the two ratios with no application to a growing firm. Level 2 applies it: rising sales mean more inventory and more trade receivables before any cash returns, so growth consumes working capital — at these figures, growing 50% would need about $105,000 of extra funding. Level 3 builds competing chains: against the importance of liquidity, that cash held is cash not invested, that a strong order book improves access to borrowing, and that profitability is what makes the business worth keeping alive at all. Level 4 reaches a supported judgement, which is what Appendix 6 states the command word requires — for example that liquidity management is decisive for this firm specifically because failure is an event of a single day while low profitability is a condition that can be worked on over a year, with the judgement supported by the firm's own figures rather than asserted. A conclusion that repeats the arguments without deciding between them is not a judgement.

practice.question: A tile wholesaler with rising revenue closes after failing to pay a supplier. Weak cash flow, overestimation of sales, overtrading, poor inventory control are all suggested. Assess the likely internal causes of its failure. (10 marks)
practice.guidance:
The trap in a case like this is treating the closure as the cause. Separate what finally happened from what made it possible, and be careful with the rising revenue: it is evidence for one of the candidate causes rather than evidence against all of them. The command word asks you to weigh the candidates against each other, so you need a reason for preferring one.
Level 1 names internal causes from the specification with no reference to the case. Level 2 applies them: rising revenue with a payment failure points towards growth outrunning the working capital rather than towards falling demand. Level 3 weighs the candidates against one another — overtrading and weak cash flow management are hard to separate, since the second is how the first becomes fatal, while overestimation of sales and poor inventory control would both show as goods unsold rather than as revenue rising. Level 4 reaches the supported judgement Appendix 6 states the command word requires: which cause was decisive, why the evidence in the case favours it, and what would have had to be true for one of the others to be the answer instead. Listing all six causes with a sentence each cannot reach the upper levels, because nothing has been weighed.

practice.question: A wholesaler that nearly closed last year after a supplier stopped delivering can either improve its liquidity or improve its profitability over the next twelve months, but does not have the management time to do both. Evaluate which it should prioritise if it is to avoid business failure. (20 marks)
practice.guidance:
This is a choice, so the answer has to end with one. Build both cases properly before deciding: what improving each one would actually involve, what it would cost, and how quickly it would work. Watch for the fact that some actions affect both, and for the difference between a problem that closes a business and a problem that makes it a poor business — those are not the same kind of urgency.
The internal and external causes of failure are the frame for this question rather than a separate topic: overtrading, poor management of cash flow, poor inventory control and supplier problems all end at the same moment, which is an invoice falling due that cannot be paid, while exchange rates and interest rates change what the firm earns without changing whether it can pay this week.
Level 1 describes liquidity and profitability separately with no reference to the choice. Level 2 applies each to the firm. Level 3 develops both cases against each other: for liquidity, that a firm closes on the day it cannot pay whatever its profit, that cutting inventory towards 30 days of cover or factoring receivables releases cash quickly, and that liquidity decides whether an unforecastable shock is survived; for profitability, that liquidity fixes are largely one-off while a better margin generates cash every year afterwards, that several of the liquidity moves carry a permanent cost such as a factor's fee or the fragility of holding very little inventory, and that a business which is not profitable is not worth rescuing. Level 4 reaches the perceptive conclusion Appendix 6 states the command word requires: a recommendation that separates the two by urgency and by permanence, notices that inventory control improves both at once and is therefore the first move whichever way the answer goes, and says what would change the recommendation — which here is how close the acid test is to saying the firm may not survive the year.

flashcards.front: What are the three profits, and what comes off at each step?
flashcards.back: Gross profit = revenue − cost of sales; Operating profit = gross profit − other operating expenses; Profit for the year = operating profit − interest. Nothing else comes off, and the specification's own statement has no tax line.

flashcards.front: Define gross profit.
flashcards.back: Revenue less cost of sales: what is left once the goods that were actually sold have been paid for. Wages, rent and marketing are not in it.

flashcards.front: Define operating profit.
flashcards.back: Gross profit less other operating expenses. It is the whole trading operation before the cost of borrowing, which is why it is the fair line for comparing two firms.

flashcards.front: Define profit for the year.
flashcards.back: Operating profit less interest. The specification also calls it net profit, and both names appear on data tables. It is what is left for the owners.

flashcards.front: What is the statement of comprehensive income?
flashcards.back: The profit ladder written out as a document, covering a period of trading rather than a single date. The specification prints the older name beside it: statement of comprehensive income (profit and loss account).

flashcards.front: Why can a data table with no interest figure not produce a profit for the year?
flashcards.back: Because interest is the only thing taken off at that step. The last figure such a table supports is the operating profit, and inventing an interest line to go further is answering a question the data could not ask.

flashcards.front: Give the three profitability formulae.
flashcards.back: Gross profit margin = (gross profit ÷ revenue) × 100. Operating profit margin = (operating profit ÷ revenue) × 100. Profit for the year margin = (profit for the year ÷ revenue) × 100. Revenue is underneath all three.

flashcards.front: What does the gap between the gross and operating margins measure?
flashcards.back: The other operating expenses, as a share of revenue. At Lantana Tiles the margins are 35% and 10%, so running the business costs 25% of every dollar taken.

flashcards.front: What does the gap between the operating and final margins measure?
flashcards.back: The cost of borrowing. Here it is 2% of revenue, which is the $40,000 of interest on a $500,000 loan. A firm that has borrowed nothing has no gap at all.

flashcards.front: What are the three ways to increase profits?
flashcards.back: Charge more, sell more, or spend less. A price rise reaches profit in full; extra sales bring their own costs; spending less lifts either the gross or the operating line depending on which cost was cut.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between profit and profitability?
flashcards.back: Profit is an amount and profitability is a rate. Cutting a price and selling far more can raise the first and lower the second at the same time: more dollars kept, less of each dollar kept.

flashcards.front: Why is profit not the same as cash?
flashcards.back: Profit is recorded when a sale is made or a cost is incurred; cash moves when money changes hands, on a different day. Selling on credit, buying inventory, buying assets and repaying loans all separate the two.

flashcards.front: Name four things that take cash without reducing profit.
flashcards.back: Buying inventory not yet sold; buying a non-current asset outright; repaying the sum borrowed on a loan; paying an invoice recorded as a cost in an earlier year. Only the interest on a loan is a cost.

flashcards.front: What is the statement of financial position?
flashcards.back: A list of what a business owns and owes on one date. Non-current assets plus current assets, less current liabilities, less non-current liabilities, gives net assets.

flashcards.front: What does "current" mean on a statement of financial position?
flashcards.back: Within twelve months, on both sides. Current assets become cash within a year; current liabilities fall due within a year. Every liquidity measure in this topic uses only those two totals.

flashcards.front: Name the current assets and the current liabilities.
flashcards.back: Current assets: inventory, trade receivables, cash. Current liabilities: trade payables, bank overdraft, other payables. Appendix 8 settles the vocabulary, because the paper uses International Accounting Standards terminology.

flashcards.front: Define working capital.
flashcards.back: Current assets less current liabilities. At Lantana Tiles that is $400,000 less $250,000, or $150,000 — almost none of which can actually be spent, because most of it is tiles and unpaid invoices.

flashcards.front: Describe the working capital cycle.
flashcards.back: Cash buys inventory; inventory is sold and becomes trade receivables; trade receivables are collected and become cash. Roughly 67 days plus 27 days from paying for goods to being paid for them.

flashcards.front: Why does a growing business need more cash rather than less?
flashcards.back: Because every extra sale puts money into inventory and into what customers owe before any of it comes back. Growing 50% at these figures would need about $105,000 of extra funding first.

flashcards.front: Give the two liquidity formulae.
flashcards.back: Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities. Acid test ratio = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities. Appendix 9 also calls the second one the liquid capital ratio, and neither is supplied in the examination.

flashcards.front: Why is inventory excluded from the acid test?
flashcards.back: Because it still has to be sold to somebody before it becomes money. Trade receivables are sales already made and cash is already money; inventory is the one current asset with another transaction still to come.

flashcards.front: What does the gap between the two liquidity ratios tell you?
flashcards.back: How much of the firm's comfort depends on selling what it is holding. Lantana Tiles shows 1.60:1 and 0.64:1, and the whole difference is $240,000 of tiles, about 67 days of cover.

flashcards.front: Name the four ways to improve liquidity the specification gives.
flashcards.back: Selling assets, extending supplier credit terms, factoring, and inventory JIT. They are four different actions with four different effects, not a ranked list.

flashcards.front: What does selling an underused asset do to liquidity?
flashcards.back: Everything improves, because something that was not a current asset became one: cash to $130,000, working capital to $270,000, the ratios to 2.08:1 and 1.12:1. The cost is the capacity given up.

flashcards.front: What does extending supplier credit terms actually change?
flashcards.back: The bank balance, and not the working capital: cash and trade payables rise by the same $106,849, so the subtraction is unchanged. The current ratio falls to 1.42:1, because adding equal amounts to both sides drags any ratio towards one to one.

flashcards.front: What does factoring do, and what is odd about its effect?
flashcards.back: A factor buys the trade receivables and pays now, less a fee. Cash goes to $155,500, but one quick asset has become another minus the fee, so the acid test edges DOWN to 0.62:1. Being able to pay and scoring well on a ratio are different things.

flashcards.front: What does inventory JIT do to the two ratios?
flashcards.back: Nothing to the current ratio and a great deal to the acid test: tiles become cash, both are current assets, and only one of them is counted in the stricter measure. Here it moves from 0.64:1 to 1.17:1. The cost is having no buffer against a late supplier.

flashcards.front: Name the six internal causes of business failure.
flashcards.back: Poor management of cash flow, overestimation of sales, overtrading, poor inventory control, poor marketing, poor quality. The first is listed first because it is how most of the others become fatal.

flashcards.front: Name the eight external causes of business failure.
flashcards.back: market conditions, competition, economic, exchange rates, interest rates, government regulations, supplier problems, natural phenomena. None is inside the firm's control, and what decides the outcome is how long it can keep paying while disrupted.

flashcards.front: Define overtrading.
flashcards.back: Growing faster than the working capital can fund it. Revenue rises, inventory and trade receivables rise with it, and the cash arrives after the costs. It is the cause of failure that happens to firms whose order books are full.

flashcards.front: Why does a price cut do more damage than a larger fall in volume?
flashcards.back: Because no cost falls with it. A 5% price cut at Lantana Tiles takes operating profit to $100,000; a 10% fall in volume, twice the size, leaves $130,000, because cost of sales falls alongside the revenue.

flashcards.front: Which cause of failure leaves the operating profit untouched, and why?
flashcards.back: A rise in interest rates. Interest is taken off between operating profit and profit for the year, so a firm hit by rates is trading exactly as well as it was: $200,000 of operating profit and $140,000 instead of $160,000.

flashcards.front: How does a currency movement reach an importer's accounts?
flashcards.back: Through cost of sales. A 10% fall in the home currency takes it from $1,300,000 to $1,430,000 and operating profit from $200,000 to $70,000. The same movement helps an exporter, at the top line.

flashcards.front: What is the one thing every cause of business failure ends in?
flashcards.back: An invoice falling due that the business cannot pay. That is why liquidity, rather than profit, decides which of two identical firms survives the same shock.

mistakes.title: Treating net profit and operating profit as the same figure
mistakes.looks_like: "Net profit, also called operating profit, is revenue minus cost of sales minus expenses."
mistakes.why: The specification's ladder puts interest between them. Operating profit is before interest; profit for the year, which is the same line as net profit, is after it. The two are the same number only for a business that has borrowed nothing, and Lantana Tiles shows $200,000 against $160,000.
mistakes.instead: Fix the vocabulary once: gross, then operating, then profit for the year (net profit). When a data table gives no interest figure, the last profit it can support is the operating profit.

mistakes.title: Putting overheads into cost of sales
mistakes.looks_like: "Cost of sales is everything the business spent to make the sales: the goods, the wages and the warehouse rent."
mistakes.why: Cost of sales is only what the goods that were sold cost to obtain. Adding the running costs produces a "gross profit" that is really an operating profit, and then the next subtraction takes the same costs off twice.
mistakes.instead: Ask of each cost: would it be owed if no goods had been sold at all? If yes, it belongs below the gross profit line.

mistakes.title: Using profit and profitability as synonyms
mistakes.looks_like: "The firm can improve profitability by growing, because bigger firms make more profit."
mistakes.why: Profit is an amount; profitability is a rate. Cutting a price and selling far more raises the first and lowers the second, because revenue and cost of sales grow together while the share of each dollar kept shrinks.
mistakes.instead: Read which of the two the question asked for. If it says profitability, the answer is about a margin, and growth is as likely to lower it as to raise it.

mistakes.title: Assuming a profitable business must be accumulating money
mistakes.looks_like: "It cannot have run out of cash, because the accounts show a profit for the year."
mistakes.why: Profit is recorded when a sale is made; cash moves when money changes hands. Lantana Tiles earned $160,000 and its bank balance moved by −$100,000, because inventory and trade receivables rose, a $100,000 asset was bought outright and $80,000 of loan was repaid.
mistakes.instead: Treat the two documents as answering different questions. The statement of comprehensive income says whether the trade is worth doing; the statement of financial position says whether the firm can still be trading next month.

mistakes.title: Applying a two-to-one rule to every current ratio
mistakes.looks_like: "The current ratio is 1.4:1, which is below the ideal of 2:1, so the business is in trouble."
mistakes.why: The specification asks for calculation and interpretation, and the interpretation is about this firm. What matters is what the current assets are made of and how fast they turn into money — a wholesaler holding two months of goods needs far more cover than a shop that sells for cash the same afternoon.
mistakes.instead: Quote both ratios and say what the gap between them is made of. That is a statement about the business; a comparison with a remembered number is not.

mistakes.title: Writing that longer supplier credit improves working capital
mistakes.looks_like: "Taking an extra month to pay suppliers increases working capital, because the cash stays in the business."
mistakes.why: Cash and trade payables rise by the same amount, so the subtraction gives exactly the same answer: $150,000, unchanged. What improves is the bank balance. The current ratio actually falls, from 1.60:1 to 1.42:1, because adding equal amounts to both sides of a ratio drags it towards one to one.
mistakes.instead: Work out both sides before claiming a direction. A move that adds to current assets and current liabilities together cannot change working capital at all.

mistakes.title: Blaming an external cause and stopping there
mistakes.looks_like: "The business failed because of the downturn in construction."
mistakes.why: Every firm in the trade faced the same conditions and some of them are still open. The external event is the trigger; what decides the outcome is the position it landed on — how much cash was held, how much was owed within the year, how much was tied up in goods.
mistakes.instead: Name the external cause, then say what internal weakness made it fatal here. A question about failure is asking for the second half, and an answer that stops at the first has given the easier one.
